content: Flat feet, also known as pes planus or fallen arches, is a condition where the arch of the foot collapses, causing the entire sole of the foot to come into full or nearly full contact with the ground. In some individuals, the arch never develops, either in one foot (unilateral) or both feet (bilateral). This condition affects an estimated 20-30% of the general population. Importantly, having flat feet does not impair foot speed. In infants, flat feet are a normal and common occurrence. This is partly due to the presence of baby fat, which obscures the developing arch, and partly because the arch has not yet fully formed. The human foot arch typically develops during infancy and early childhood as muscles, tendons, ligaments, and bones grow. Activities such as foot gymnastics and walking barefoot on varied terrain can promote the development of arches in children. By the age of four to six years, most children have a fully developed arch. Parents or caregivers should monitor children for signs of flat feet, as young children are unlikely to recognize or report the condition themselves. Visual inspection is helpful, but parents should also observe for unusual walking patterns, such as walking on the outer edges of the feet or limping during long walks. Additionally, children may report foot pain, sometimes described as a sensation similar to a nail piercing the foot, or calf muscle pain, which could indicate flat feet. Recent medical studies suggest that arch support inserts and specific heel cups placed in a growing child’s shoes can aid in the proper development of the longitudinal arch. These devices help maintain the foot in a neutral position during growth. However, there is strong evidence that walking barefoot, especially on uneven surfaces like sand, strengthens foot muscles and promotes arch development. A study conducted in India found that children who grew up walking barefoot had stronger and higher arches compared to those who wore closed-toe shoes. Children who wore sandals or slippers also had a lower prevalence of flat feet compared to those who wore closed-toe footwear. Flat feet can also develop in adulthood, a condition referred to as adult-acquired flatfoot. This can result from injury, illness, prolonged stress on the foot, faulty biomechanics, or the natural aging process. Pregnant women may temporarily develop flat feet due to increased levels of elastin, which enhances tissue elasticity during pregnancy. However, if flat feet develop in adulthood, they are generally permanent. In some cases, individuals may appear flatfooted when standing in a weight-bearing position, but an arch becomes visible when they dorsiflex (stand on tiptoes or pull the toes back while keeping the rest of the foot flat on the ground). This is known as flexible flatfoot. While foot muscle training can be beneficial, it is unlikely to increase arch height in adults because the muscles in the foot are too short to significantly change with exercise. However, in children whose feet are still growing, there remains a possibility of creating a lasting arch. A podiatrist can diagnose flat feet during a routine office visit. A simple home test, known as the wet foot test, involves wetting the feet and standing on a surface like cement or heavy paper. If the footprint shows no dry area where the arch should be, this suggests flat feet. Most cases of flexible flat feet are asymptomatic and do not cause pain, so they are not typically a cause for concern. However, rigid flatfoot, where the sole remains flat even when not weight-bearing, may require medical attention. Certain conditions associated with flat feet, such as tarsal coalition (abnormal fusion of two or more bones in the midfoot or hindfoot) or an accessory navicular (an extra bone on the side of the foot), should be addressed early, ideally before the bones fully mature in the teenage years. These conditions can be confirmed through X-rays. Treatment for flat feet may also be necessary if the condition causes pain in the feet, lower legs, knees, or back. Management options include the use of arch supports or orthotics, foot exercises, or other interventions recommended by a podiatrist or physician. In severe cases, surgery may be considered to provide lasting relief or even create an arch, though it is typically expensive and reserved as a last resort. Studies on the relationship between arch height and stress fractures have yielded mixed results. One study of 287 Israeli Defense Force recruits found that individuals with high arches experienced nearly four times as many stress fractures as those with low arches. However, a later study of 449 U.S. naval special warfare trainees found no significant difference in stress fracture rates based on arch height, and another study was inconclusive.
